title: No Model Required: Text Entropy Rate FilteringMitigates Iterative Fine-Tuning Collapse

paper.title: No Model Required: Text Entropy Rate Filtering Mitigates Iterative Fine-Tuning Collapse
paper.abstract:
Abstract Iterative fine-tuning on synthetic data causes model collapse : output
diversity narrows as rare patterns are progressively lost, a signature most
visible as phrase-level repetition. Existing
mitigations either require model log-probabilities, an external oracle, or continued
access to real human data. Here we develop a new approach grounded in mathematical information theory: the non-parametric Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , computed entirely from raw text via match-length statistics, with no
model of any kind. We show that this is in fact a superior training-data filter on text-diversity
metrics in a fully-synthetic, single-lineage fine-tuning setting.
In a six-generation QLoRA collapse experiment on
Llama-3.1-8B, logprob-based filtering (the most established model-access-requiring baseline) provides
no significant text-diversity benefit on any metric ( p > 0.23 p>0.23 ), whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering yields + 42 % +42\% unique trigrams, + 30 % +30\% vocabulary, and − 19 % -19\% repetition (all p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). We validate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a cross-domain
entropy proxy ( β = 0.924 \beta=0.924 , R 2 = 0.746 R^{2}=0.746 ) and collapse detector
( ρ = + 0.454 \rho=+0.454 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ) across 4 domains, 2 temperatures,
2 generator–scorer model pairs, and 1,520 generated documents.
Our results demonstrate that information theoretic approaches to collapse mitigation are efficient, and suggest new approaches for maintaining multi-agent diversity.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models trained on their own outputs face a self-reinforcing degradation known as model collapse : when a model’s outputs are used to fine-tune successor models, the entropy of the output distribution declines across generations, diversity narrows, and rare linguistic patterns are progressively lost ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ) . As synthetic content becomes an increasing fraction of web-scraped training corpora, collapse mitigation is shifting from a theoretical concern to an engineering requirement for production training pipelines. Existing mitigations for model collapse fall into one of three categories: (A) model logprob filters such as surplexity filtering ( Gambetta et al., 2026 ) , which scores documents by the model’s own per-token Shannon entropy and retains those the model finds surprising; (B) external oracle or classifier approaches utilising an independent language model; and (C) data accumulation strategies that re-inject real human data at each generation ( Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Bertrand et al., 2024 ) . Among filtering approaches that do not require the injection of real, expensive human data, surplexity filtering is the most established model-access-requiring baseline. Gambetta et al. (2026) demonstrate that it delays collapse as measured by the model’s own entropy and perplexity scores, but its effect on independent text-diversity measures has not been evaluated. Throughout this paper we compare against mean per-token Shannon entropy H L H_{L} specifically, which is closely related to but not necessarily identical to surplexity: both are monotonically increasing functions of the model’s output entropy, but surplexity uses the sample surprise of the generated tokens whereas H L H_{L} averages over the full output distribution, so the two induce highly similar but not necessarily identical document rankings. Moreover, Guo et al. (2024) find that linguistic acceptability filtering can actually worsen collapse, underscoring that the choice of filtering criterion is consequential. Surplexity filtering requires a forward pass through the model being trained, with access to the full next-token distribution at each position. Such access is unavailable for closed-source APIs, computationally expensive at scale, and version-dependent – the same document receives different surplexity scores as the model is updated. Data accumulation avoids model access but presupposes a continuing supply of human-authored text, which is costly and slow to generate, and unavailable in a fully synthetic closed loop. A text-only collapse filter that requires no model of any kind would be strictly preferable, even if it were found to be less effective than surplexity filtering. Motivated by results from mathematical information theory, we propose the Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ( Kontoyiannis et al., 1998 ) as a text-only collapse filter and show that it outperforms logprob-based filtering. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} estimates the entropy rate of a symbolic sequence by measuring match lengths: at each position, it records the length of the longest prefix of the remaining text that has previously appeared in the document. Long matches signal repetition in the text; short matches signal novelty. The Kontoyiannis estimator has previously been used to quantify information flow in social media text ( Bagrow et al., 2019 ; Bagrow and Mitchell, 2018 ; Pond et al., 2020 ) and requires no model, no API, and no GPU. To our knowledge, no prior work has applied H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} or any compression-rate statistic as a collapse filter; it is the only proposed filter of this type requiring no model of any kind – not a forward pass, not an oracle, not a reference classifier. Figure 1 : Filtering on text-only entropy preserves diversity; logprob-based filtering does not. (a) Kontoyiannis entropy rate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} across six fine-tuning generations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under three training-data conditions: unfiltered (rapid collapse), H L H_{L} -filtered (intermediate), and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtered (slowest decline). Shaded bands: ± 1 \pm 1 SEM ( n = 80 n=80 documents per generation). (b) Percentage change relative to the unfiltered baseline at generation 6 for three text-diversity metrics (Distinct-3, Vocabulary size, Rep-4). Error bars: bootstrap 95% CIs. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -based filtering yields highly significant improvements on all three metrics ( ∗ ∗ ∗ p < 0.001 {}^{***}p<0.001 ), whereas H L H_{L} -based filtering is non-significant on all three. Figure 1 previews our central result. In a six-generation QLoRA fine-tuning experiment on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) , each generation’s model is fine-tuned from the previous one – a continuous model lineage reflecting the realistic deployed scenario – and the filter operates in a fully synthetic closed loop with no human data available for re-injection. H L H_{L} -based training-data filtering – the most established model-access-requiring baseline – provides no significant text-diversity benefit on any measured metric ( p > 0.23 p>0.23 ), whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -based filtering yields highly significant improvements ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) on Distinct-3, vocabulary size, and repetition rate – despite H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} requiring no model access at all. The two filters select substantially different training documents (mean within-domain Jaccard similarity ≈ 0.35 \approx 0.35 ), indicating that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is not merely approximating surplexity but operating on a complementary axis: resistance to phrase-level repetition, the primary surface manifestation of fine-tuning collapse. We validate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} through three experiments: establishing it as a proxy for logprob entropy across domains, temperatures, and model pairs (Section 3 ); characterising when it does and does not track collapse (Section 4 ); and demonstrating that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -based filtering outperforms logprob-based filtering in a controlled iterative fine-tuning experiment (Section 5 ). We release our code and data for reproducibility 1 1 1 https://github.com/lewismath/no-model-required .

sections.heading: Model collapse.
sections.text: Shumailov et al. (2024) demonstrate that iterative training on model-generated data causes progressive loss of distributional tails: output variance shrinks across generations as the model reinforces its existing biases. The phenomenon is formalised by Alemohammad et al. (2024) , who show that without real-data anchoring, iterative self-distillation inevitably converges to low-entropy output. Briesch et al. (2023) provide the first LLM-specific empirical study of self-consuming training loops, finding that diversity declines in proportion to the synthetic data fraction. Measuring collapse in terms of text-level diversity is a more recent development: Guo et al. (2024) conduct iterative fine-tuning on NLG tasks and track lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity across generations, observing that syntactic diversity deteriorates fastest and creative tasks are most vulnerable. Both works characterise collapse through output distribution statistics; we measure it directly via the entropy rate of the generated text. Analogous diversity collapse has been documented in multi-agent LLM systems, where structural coupling during iterative interaction drives premature semantic convergence even without any weight update ( Chen et al., 2026 ) ; the present work identifies a complementary mechanism operating through the fine-tuning data loop.

sections.heading: Mitigating model collapse.
sections.text: Existing mitigations fall into three broad categories, each imposing a distinct requirement on the practitioner. (A) Model-logprob methods. Gambetta et al. (2026) propose surplexity – the product of token-level surprise and perplexity – as a data-quality signal for collapse mitigation. In practice, retaining high-surplexity documents is closely related to filtering by the mean Shannon entropy of the generator’s next-token distribution, which we denote H L H_{L} . This is the text-level analogue of perplexity-based data filtering widely used in large-scale pretraining pipelines ( Wenzek et al., 2020 ) . Zhu et al. (2025) resample tokens whose predicted probability exceeds a threshold from a prior language model, requiring token-level logprobs during generation, while Alemohammad et al. (2024) show that biased or top- K K sampling – retaining only the highest-scoring synthetic samples each generation – can slow collapse when a quality score derived from model internals is available. All three methods require access to the generating model’s output distribution. (B) External-oracle methods. Feng et al. (2025) argue that scaling up with synthesised data requires an external verifier – a stronger model or human annotator – to score and filter synthetic samples. Yi et al. (2025) extend this line with convergence guarantees for verifier-based filtering, but identify a critical caveat: long-run convergence is toward the verifier’s biased knowledge centre, not the true data distribution, unless the verifier is perfect. This finding motivates the search for estimators that introduce no external model bias. (C) Real-data accumulation. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) prove that accumulating all prior real and synthetic data yields a finite error bound and validate this empirically. Bertrand et al. (2024) show that retaining a fixed fraction of real data each generation guarantees stability, and Fu et al. (2025) establish that even a constant proportion of real data ensures convergence in transformers. All three approaches require continued access to human-authored data at each training round. Each type of mitigation thus requires either model internals (A), a stronger external model (B), or curated human data (C), imposing an extra burden to mitigate model collapse regardless of the approach taken. In this work we introduce a novel filter in category (D): H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is computed from raw text alone – no model, no API, no GPU, no reference corpus – making it, to our knowledge, the only completely model-free and reference-free model collapse filter proposed to date.

sections.heading: Relationship to data deduplication.
sections.text: Min-hash near-deduplication ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Penedo et al., 2024 ) is the standard model-free text-quality filter in large-scale pretraining pipelines, and is the one existing method that, like H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering, requires neither model access nor an external verifier. It removes near-duplicate documents from the training corpus (a between-document operation), whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering selects documents by within-document phrase variety (a within-document operation). The two approaches are complementary: deduplication prevents the corpus from containing many copies of the same text, while H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering ensures each document has not collapsed into internally repetitive structure. A combined pipeline (deduplicate first, then H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter) would address both failure modes.

sections.heading: The Kontoyiannis estimator.
sections.text: Kontoyiannis et al. (1998) prove that the estimator H ^ K = n ​ log 2 ​ n ∑ i = 1 n Λ i \hat{H}_{K}=\frac{n\log_{2}n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Lambda_{i}} (1) converges almost surely to the entropy rate H H of any stationary ergodic process – no parametric assumptions on the token distribution are required – where Λ i \Lambda_{i} is the length of the shortest prefix of x i , … , x n x_{i},\ldots,x_{n} that does not appear as a contiguous substring in x 1 , … , x i − 1 x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1} ; near the end of a document, where no such non-appearing prefix may exist, Λ i \Lambda_{i} is bounded by the remaining sequence length n − i n-i , so the sum in Equation ( 1 ) remains well-defined without special-casing. Reported H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} values use the ProcessEntropy package’s tokenizer 2 2 2 https://github.com/tobinsouth/ProcessEntropy : an NLTK TweetTokenizer pass, lower-cased, with non-alphanumeric characters stripped from within each token ( South et al., 2022 ) . Real-time filtering decisions during fine-tuning (Section 5 ) instead use a faster whitespace tokenization (lower-case; non-alphanumeric characters replaced with whitespace) for computational efficiency; the two agree closely in practice (Spearman ρ = 0.997 \rho=0.997 on a held-out sample), so the choice does not affect which documents are selected. The estimator’s consistency is grounded in the Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem ( Cover and Thomas, 2006 ) : for a stationary ergodic source, − 1 n ​ log 2 ⁡ P ⁡ ( X 1 , … , X n ) → H -\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}P(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\to H almost surely, and Λ i \Lambda_{i} serves as a nonparametric proxy for local self-information at position i i – long matches signal low surprise; short matches signal high surprise. The match lengths also connect H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} to Lempel–Ziv (LZ) data compression ( Ziv and Lempel, 1977 ; Ziv and Lempel, 1978 ) : each Λ i \Lambda_{i} identifies the shortest phrase at position i i not resolvable from prior context – the elementary step of LZ parsing – so H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is interpretable as a normalised LZ compression rate. While compression-based statistics have been used for general data quality assessment, to our knowledge no prior work has applied H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} or any LZ-derived metric as a model collapse mitigation filter. At finite n n , H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is upward-biased: early positions have little past context, so Λ i \Lambda_{i} is artificially small and the denominator is deflated. We control for this by computing H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} on the first 1,500 word tokens of each document and discarding shorter texts (see Section 3 ); the residual finite-sample bias is reported as a limitation in Section 6 . The Kontoyiannis estimator provides a model-free measure of sequential complexity that depends only on the text itself ( Bagrow et al., 2019 ; Smart et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Fine-tuning.
sections.text: We use QLoRA ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) – 4-bit NF4 quantisation with low-rank adaptation ( Hu et al., 2022 ) – for all fine-tuning experiments. QLoRA makes multi-generation fine-tuning tractable on a single A100 GPU, enabling the iterative collapse and filtering experiments described in Sections 4 and 5 .

sections.heading: 3 H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a Proxy for Logprob Entropy
sections.text: We first ask whether H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is a suitable proxy for H L H_{L} , by comparing the two metrics on a set of synthetic documents.

sections.heading: 3.1 Cross-domain and cross-temperature validation
sections.text: We generated 200 documents using GPT-4o across 4 domains (encyclopedic, creative, scientific, conversational), 2 temperatures ( T ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 } T\in\{0.5,1.0\} ; higher temperatures were excluded in preliminary testing because too large a fraction of sampled tokens fell outside the top-20 returned logprobs), and 25 topics per domain; 197 documents passed a reliability filter requiring that fewer than 5% of a document’s tokens have unrecoverable (invalid) logprob coverage. For each document we computed H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} via Equation ( 1 ) applied to the first 1,500 word tokens, and H L H_{L} , the mean per-token Shannon entropy of the generator’s next-token distribution, renormalised over the top-20 returned logprobs. An OLS regression of H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} on H L H_{L} with domain fixed effects yields β = 0.924 \beta=0.924 ( R 2 = 0.746 R^{2}=0.746 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ; Figure 2 a shows the T = 1.0 T=1.0 subset). A likelihood-ratio test for domain-specific slopes fails to reject equality ( p = 0.41 p=0.41 ), confirming a domain-invariant slope : the relationship between H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} is consistent across domains up to a domain-level intercept offset. Domains differ in baseline entropy – creative and conversational text is more varied; scientific text more constrained – but H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} scales with H L H_{L} at the same rate in each. The domain-invariant slope has a practical consequence for data filtering. Because filtering requires only the rank order of documents by entropy (selecting the top- k k ), not absolute calibration, a single H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} computation suffices for within-domain ranking. In a mixed-domain corpus, domain stratification remains necessary to prevent over-selection from naturally higher-entropy domains.

sections.heading: 3.2 Cross-model validation
sections.text: The cross-domain experiments above use the same model (GPT-4o) for both generation and H L H_{L} scoring. Here we test whether the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} / H L H_{L} relationship holds when H L H_{L} is computed by a different model family altogether. We generated additional corpora using Gemini 1.5 Pro ( Gemini Team, Google, 2024 ) and scored all documents – both GPT-4o-generated and Gemini-generated – using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) as an independent scorer. Both the GPT-4o/Qwen and Gemini/Qwen pairings reproduce the positive H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} / H L H_{L} relationship (Figure 2 b), confirming that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} measures a property of the text itself, not of any particular model’s distribution over that text.

sections.heading: 3.3 Scope: proxy validity on collapse-experiment data
sections.text: The validations above use text generated under controlled conditions (varied temperature, well-distributed topics). To assess whether the relationship extends to the data used in the collapse experiment itself, we compute H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} on the 80 generation-0 documents produced by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (the base model, before any fine-tuning). The correlation is near zero and non-significant ( r = 0.18 r=0.18 , p = 0.11 p=0.11 , n = 80 n=80 ). This is not a failure of the estimator but a known property of the base model’s output distribution: as documented in Figure 8 , the base Llama model produces a wide bimodal H L H_{L} distribution (SD = 2.17) driven by topic-dependent familiarity rather than document-level diversity. Within each topic, H L H_{L} is nearly constant; between topics it varies by up to 7 bits. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , which measures within-document phrase variety, is orthogonal to this between-topic variation. The proxy relationship holds when H L H_{L} reflects genuine document-level entropy variation, but not when it is dominated by topic-familiarity confounds – and this is the root cause of H L H_{L} -filtering’s failure in Section 5 . (a) Cross-domain validation: GPT-4o corpus ( T = 1.0 T=1.0 , n = 97 n=97 ). (b) Cross-model validation: GPT-4o and Gemini corpora, both scored by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Figure 2 : H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} versus H L H_{L} across domains and model pairs. Points are coloured by domain. The slope is domain-invariant in both panels: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} scales with H L H_{L} at a consistent rate regardless of domain, generating model, or scoring model.

sections.heading: 4 Detecting Model Collapse Without Logprobs
sections.text: Having established H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a cross-sectional proxy for H L H_{L} , we next ask whether it tracks collapse over generations . Under iterative rephrasing, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} co-decline at indistinguishable rates ( δ = − 0.004 \delta=-0.004 , p = 0.59 p=0.59 ), but within-generation rank concordance is near zero (Spearman ρ ≈ 0 \rho\approx 0 ), as rephrasing homogenises surface statistics across documents and eliminates the variance needed to discriminate between estimators. The fine-tuning regime is more informative, as we explore below.

sections.heading: 4.1 Iterative fine-tuning collapse
sections.text: Fine-tuning collapse operates through a different mechanism than rephrasing. Rather than paraphrasing existing content, the model’s generative style drifts: text exhibits increased phrase repetition, reduced vocabulary diversity, and narrower syntactic range (see examples in Appendix A ). We conducted a 6-generation QLoRA fine-tuning experiment (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, unfiltered training data) and computed within-topic H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} / H L H_{L} concordance across generations for each of 39 topics (one topic was excluded due to insufficient within-generation variance for reliable rank correlation). Under fine-tuning collapse, within-topic Spearman concordance is ρ = + 0.454 \rho=+0.454 ( p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ), with 30 of 39 topics showing positive concordance (Figure 3 b). This contrasts sharply with the rephrasing scenario ( ρ = − 0.175 \rho=-0.175 , non-significant). The explanation is that fine-tuning collapse changes the surface statistics of generated text in ways H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} directly measures – repetitive phrase structure, reduced n n -gram diversity – whereas rephrasing preserves the within-generation homogeneity that masks both estimators. This result establishes H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a valid detector of fine-tuning collapse specifically, and motivates its use as a filter in that regime. (a) Iterative rephrasing collapse: mean ± \pm SEM of H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} across rephrasing generations. Both estimators decline together ( δ = − 0.004 \delta=-0.004 , p = 0.59 p=0.59 ). Shaded region: gen-0 reference (length-mismatched). (b) Iterative fine-tuning collapse: within-topic Spearman ρ \rho under fine-tuning collapse. Each point is one topic; diamonds show domain means. Figure 3 : H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a collapse detector under two regimes. Under rephrasing (a), H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} co-decline but within-generation concordance is ≈ 0 \approx 0 . Under fine-tuning (b), within-topic concordance is strongly positive ( ρ = + 0.454 \rho=+0.454 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ), driven by phrase-level repetition that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} directly measures.

sections.heading: 5 H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a Training Data Filter
sections.text: Having established that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is a good collapse detector, we now consider our central question: can H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} be used to filter training data and mitigate collapse; and, if so, does it outperform H L H_{L} , the most established model-access-requiring baseline?

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental design
sections.text: We run three parallel 6-generation QLoRA fine-tuning chains on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. At each generation, 80 documents are generated across 4 domains (10 topics × \times 2 documents per topic per domain); 40 are selected for training according to the condition: Unfiltered : random selection (seed fixed per generation); H L H_{L} -filter : top 40 by mean per-token Shannon entropy (logprob-based surplexity; see Section 1 for the distinction between H L H_{L} and surplexity proper); and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter : top 40 by Kontoyiannis entropy rate (text-only). Selection is domain-stratified (10 documents per domain), so both filters operate within domain. Generation-0 documents are drawn from the base model and are shared across conditions. Training uses 4-bit NF4 QLoRA (rank 16, α = 16 \alpha=16 , learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , cosine schedule, 3 epochs per generation, effective batch size 8). Documents selected for training are truncated at the onset of 4-gram repetition; this preprocessing does not apply to generated outputs, which are evaluated as-is (see Appendix A ). The experiment produces 1,520 documents in total: 80 shared generation-0 documents plus 3 conditions × \times 6 further generations × \times 80 documents.

sections.heading: Reproducibility.
sections.text: Generation uses a fixed decoding temperature of 1.0 1.0 throughout. Prompts follow a fixed template with a domain-specific system prompt (e.g., for encyclopedic: “You are writing an encyclopaedia. Write in a neutral, factual, Wikipedia-style tone.”) and a shared user prompt, “Write a detailed, long-form piece about the following topic. Write at least 3,000 words. Do not stop early. Topic: {topic}.” The topic set (10 per domain × \times 4 domains) is identical across all six generations and across all three conditions: the only thing that varies by condition is which 40 of the 80 candidate documents are selected for training at each generation and, from generation 1 onward, which fine-tuned checkpoint generates the following round’s candidate documents.

sections.heading: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering slows collapse.
sections.text: At generation 6, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering retains 1.43 1.43 bits/word versus 0.79 0.79 for unfiltered ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) and 1.16 1.16 for H L H_{L} -filtering ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). On all three text-diversity metrics, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering produces large, significant improvements over unfiltered training: + 42 % +42\% more unique trigrams, + 30 % +30\% larger vocabulary, and − 19 % -19\% less intra-document repetition (all p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). These gains are consistent across all four domains (domain-level trajectories and full metric suites across generations are shown in Appendix B ). Illustrative generation-6 documents from the unfiltered and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter conditions are shown in Appendix A .

sections.heading: H L H_{L} -filtering provides no text-diversity benefit.
sections.text: Despite having access to the model’s log-probabilities, H L H_{L} -filtering produces no significant improvement on any of the three text-diversity metrics ( p > 0.23 p>0.23 on all). It does outperform unfiltered training on the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} metric itself ( p = 0.008 p=0.008 ), but the effect is less than half that of the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter. The failure has a clear mechanistic explanation: after even one fine-tuning step, the H L H_{L} distribution compresses dramatically (gen-0 SD = 2.17 =2.17 ; gen-1 SD = 0.13 =0.13 ), collapsing the ranking signal the filter depends on. Within a generation whose outputs are already near-uniform in H L H_{L} , the filter degenerates to near-random selection.

sections.heading: Mixed-effects analysis.
sections.text: A mixed-effects regression ( H ^ K ∼ generation × condition + ( 1 | topic ) \hat{H}_{K}\sim\text{generation}\times\text{condition}+(1|\text{topic}) , baseline: unfiltered) decomposes the trajectory into a starting-quality component and a rate-of-collapse component. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering produces a significant intercept shift ( β = + 0.37 \beta=+0.37 bits, p = 0.001 p=0.001 ); because all conditions share the same generation-0 documents, this reflects the shape of the fitted trajectories rather than a pre-existing quality difference. The slope improvement is positive but does not reach significance ( Δ ​ slope = + 0.058 \Delta\text{slope}=+0.058 bits/gen, p = 0.067 p=0.067 ). H L H_{L} -filtering produces neither a significant intercept shift nor a slope improvement ( p > 0.1 p>0.1 on both).

sections.heading: The filters select different documents.
sections.text: Within-domain Jaccard similarity between the H L H_{L} -filter and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter selection sets has a mean of 0.35 (range 0.18–0.54 across generations and domains). The two criteria do not approximate each other: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} selects on phrase-level novelty, while H L H_{L} selects on token-level model uncertainty. The success of H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering despite this low overlap suggests that phrase-level repetition, not token-level surprise, is the more informative axis for collapse mitigation – consistent with the observation that fine-tuning collapse manifests primarily in surface repetition.

sections.heading: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} outperforms simpler text-only baselines.
sections.text: A natural objection is that any per-document diversity statistic might replicate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s advantage – for instance, type–token ratio (TTR) or bigram distinctiveness (Distinct-2). We assess this by simulating both filters on the generation-0 pool, where all conditions share the same 80 documents and the comparison is exact. TTR@500-filtering selects training documents with mean H ^ K = 3.37 \hat{H}_{K}=3.37 ; Distinct-2-filtering selects mean H ^ K = 3.32 \hat{H}_{K}=3.32 ; H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering selects mean H ^ K = 3.98 \hat{H}_{K}=3.98 – a 18–20% advantage. Despite moderate positive correlations between TTR and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} in the pool (Pearson r = 0.54 r=0.54 ), the selection sets overlap only 43% by Jaccard, indicating that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} recovers phrase-level structure that per-document surface statistics do not capture. The difference is structural: TTR and Distinct-2 aggregate over short local windows, whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is sensitive to long-range match structure – precisely the property that fine-tuning collapse erodes. We repeated this static-pool comparison against two further model-free criteria: an off-the-shelf gzip-compression ratio (least-compressible 40 documents selected per domain) and an explicit 4-gram repetition-rate filter (lowest repeated-4-gram rate). Both correlate with H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} only moderately (gzip r = + 0.44 r=+0.44 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ; repetition rate r = − 0.36 r=-0.36 , p = 0.001 p=0.001 ) – comparable to the TTR correlation above – and select substantially different document sets (Jaccard 0.36 0.36 – 0.38 0.38 against the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter selection). As with the TTR/Distinct-2 comparison, this establishes that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is related to but not redundant with either criterion on the static pool, but not downstream collapse-resistance, which we test directly by running both as genuine six-generation training filters, replacing H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} in the filtering criterion but otherwise identical to Section 5 . At generation 6, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering significantly outperforms both on every metric ( H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , Distinct-3, Rep-4, vocabulary; all p < 0.005 p<0.005 , most p < 10 − 4 p<10^{-4} ). The two static-pool-comparable criteria do not perform alike as real filters, however: gzip-filtering gives a modest but genuine diversity benefit over unfiltered training (Distinct-3 + 17 % +17\% , vocabulary + 17 % +17\% , Rep-4 − 7 % -7\% ; all p < 0.03 p<0.03 ), while repetition-rate filtering gives none (all four metrics indistinguishable from unfiltered, p > 0.24 p>0.24 ) despite directly targeting repetition. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s advantage over simpler model-free heuristics is therefore not just a static-pool artefact: it persists, and in repetition-rate filtering’s case is entirely absent for the alternative, under the same six-generation training loop that constitutes this paper’s central result.

sections.heading: External validation.
sections.text: We scored gen-6 documents from all conditions using GPT-2 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) , a 124M-parameter model with no relation to training or generation pipelines. GPT-2 entropy shows the same directional ordering ( H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtered > > H L H_{L} -filtered > > unfiltered) but does not reach significance ( p = 0.11 p=0.11 ), limiting its value as independent validation; GPT-2’s discriminative power on long-form text is insufficient to detect the effect at the individual-document level. We also evaluated each generation’s fine-tuned checkpoint on HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Figure 4 b). Accuracy drops sharply from generation 0 to generation 1 ( 0.729 → ≈ 0.672 0.729\to\approx 0.672 ) and then plateaus near 0.652 0.652 – 0.657 0.657 with no significant difference between conditions at any generation. Thus H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering preserves text diversity but does not protect general reasoning ability: the capability degradation introduced by iterative fine-tuning is uniform across all three conditions. Two further downstream benchmarks corroborate this: 5-shot MMLU and 8-shot GSM8K (1,000-example subsamples each) on the same checkpoints show no significant difference between conditions at generation 6 (MMLU: 67.6 67.6 – 67.6 % 67.6\% ; GSM8K: 70.7 70.7 – 71.2 % 71.2\% ; all pairwise χ 2 \chi^{2} tests p > 0.8 p>0.8 ), nor a significant decline from generation 0 to generation 6 within any single condition ( p > 0.15 p>0.15 ) – consistent with HellaSwag, general capability retention is unaffected by which text-diversity filter is used, at this scale and over this many generations. Figure 4 : (a) H L H_{L} (logprob entropy) trajectories across six fine-tuning generations for the three filtering conditions ( ± 1 \pm 1 SEM bands). All collapse to low H L H_{L} by gen-1 and track nearly identically, illustrating why the H L H_{L} filter fails: post-collapse variance is too small to discriminate. (b) HellaSwag normalised accuracy (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) across six generations. All three conditions degrade from 0.729 0.729 (gen-0) to ≈ 0.652 \approx 0.652 – 0.657 0.657 (generation 6) with no significant difference between conditions, indicating that text-diversity preservation does not translate to preserved general reasoning ability.

sections.heading: Why H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering outperforms H L H_{L} -filtering.
sections.text: The Kontoyiannis estimator directly penalises repeated phrase structure: a document with many recurring n n -grams exhibits long match lengths and hence a low H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} . Fine-tuning collapse manifests primarily as increased phrase repetition, so H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering targets collapse’s dominant surface signature directly. H L H_{L} , by contrast, measures token-level uncertainty in the scorer model – a signal that is destroyed after a single fine-tuning step, as shown in Section 5 . At generation-0, H L H_{L} primarily reflects topic familiarity – the wide bimodal distribution documented in Figure 8 – rather than document diversity, so a criterion uncorrelated with document quality at generation-0 cannot select high-quality training data regardless of downstream variance. The result suggests that collapse is fundamentally a phrase-repetition phenomenon, and that phrase-level statistics are better positioned to detect it than token-level uncertainty. A literal reimplementation of surplexity confirms this mechanistic prediction directly: its median absolute deviation across the shared generation-0 pool is 4.40 4.40 , falling to 0.40 0.40 – 0.49 0.49 (all three conditions) after one fine-tuning step – a 9 9 – 11 11 -fold narrowing, comparable to H L H_{L} ’s own collapse. (Generation-0 surplexity is heavy-tailed – a handful of unfamiliar-topic documents receive extreme values once surprise is exponentiated into perplexity – so median and MAD, not mean and SD, are the meaningful summary here.)

sections.heading: Filter design determines direction of effect.
sections.text: Not all filters slow collapse: Guo et al. (2024) find that linguistic acceptability filtering (a RoBERTa classifier trained on CoLA) accelerates diversity decline, since such filters retain conventional, high-frequency text and discard the inventive samples most worth keeping. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering operates on the opposite principle, selecting for the phrase-level novelty that collapse erodes.

sections.heading: The Jaccard gap and Simpson’s paradox.
sections.text: The reason why the two filters select such different documents (Jaccard ≈ 0.35 \approx 0.35 ) when H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} are well-correlated at the corpus level ( R 2 = 0.746 R^{2}=0.746 ) is a form of Simpson’s paradox. The between -domain correlation is strong: creative and conversational text have both high H L H_{L} and high H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ; scientific text has both low. But within a domain and generation – which is where filtering operates, due to domain stratification – the residual correlation is near zero. The estimators measure genuinely different properties of intra-domain text variation; H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s phrase-level novelty proves more informative for collapse resistance.

sections.heading: Practical implications.
sections.text: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} filtering requires no model access, no API calls, and no GPU: scoring a 1,500-word document takes under 10 ms, and a pipeline producing 10 5 10^{5} candidate documents per round incurs negligible, trivially parallelisable overhead. This makes collapse-resistant data curation practical where logprob access is unavailable: closed-source API distillation, cross-organisation data sharing, and federated training.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Most importantly, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering preserves text diversity but does not protect general reasoning ability: HellaSwag accuracy degrades equally across all three filtering conditions (Figure 4 b), and MMLU and GSM8K show the same pattern, so our claim is scoped to distributional fidelity of generated text, not downstream task performance. The filtering advantage is also specific to fine-tuning collapse: under iterative rephrasing, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} tracks the aggregate trajectory but cannot distinguish among documents within a generation, and is therefore unsuitable as a within-generation filter in that setting. The diversity gains measured here are lexical: MAUVE scores ( Pillutla et al., 2021 ) (GPT-2-Large features, first 512 tokens) are near-ceiling and uniform across conditions at generation 6 ( 0.987 0.987 – 0.993 0.993 ), indicating embedding-space similarity is preserved and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s advantage is specific to within-document match-length structure. A separate concern is quality: selecting for match-length novelty could favour incoherent or off-topic text over genuinely diverse text. We address this directly with an LLM-judge pass (GPT-4o-mini, blind to condition) scoring all 240 generation-6 documents (80 per condition) on two 1–5 scales, coherence and instruction-following, reading the full document so that late-document degeneration is not missed. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering scores highest of the three conditions on both: coherence 2.35 2.35 versus 2.20 2.20 for unfiltered ( p = 0.058 p=0.058 ) and 2.29 2.29 for H L H_{L} -filtering; instruction-following 3.23 3.23 versus 3.00 3.00 for unfiltered ( p = 0.020 p=0.020 ) and 3.15 3.15 for H L H_{L} -filtering. If anything, then, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering’s diversity advantage comes with a small quality benefit rather than a coherence cost. Finally, our collapse experiment uses a single model family (Llama-3.1, 8B); replicating with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (same corpus and protocol), H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering again retains more diversity at generation 6 ( 2.91 2.91 bits/word versus 2.12 2.12 unfiltered, p < 0.001 p<0.001 , and 2.41 2.41 for H L H_{L} -filtering, p = 0.004 p=0.004 ; H L H_{L} -filtering again non-significant on all text-diversity metrics), with the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -vs- H L H_{L} comparison itself reaching significance on the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} metric ( p = 0.004 p=0.004 vs p = 0.088 p=0.088 at 8B), providing stronger evidence the two filters are genuinely different. Beyond replication, the Kontoyiannis cross-entropy rate h ^ × ​ ( T ∣ S ) \hat{h}_{\times}(T\mid S) is a natural complement to H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , selecting for documents that have diverged from prior-generation content; the same signal could operationalise – as an automatic, text-only proxy – the blind-writing independence phase Chen et al. (2026) identify as the most effective structural intervention against diversity collapse.

sections.heading: Broader impacts.
sections.text: The primary benefit is making collapse-resistant data curation accessible without model access, reducing a practical barrier for organisations running iterative fine-tuning under closed-source or resource-constrained conditions, and counteracting homogenisation of AI-generated web content. The main negative consequence is indirect: making fully-synthetic training pipelines more viable may reduce the incentive to collect or compensate human-authored training data; practitioners deploying such pipelines at scale should weigh this trade-off.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that the Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} – a model-free, match-length measure of sequential complexity – is an effective training-data filter against fine-tuning-driven model collapse: at generation 6 it produces 42 % 42\% more unique trigrams, 30 % 30\% larger vocabulary, and 19 % 19\% less intra-document repetition than unfiltered training, while logprob-based filtering shows no significant diversity benefit. For iterative pipelines where model internals are inaccessible, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering offers a strong, zero-cost baseline.

sections.heading: Appendix B Supplementary Figures
sections.text: This appendix provides additional figures supporting the main experimental results. The first two figures (Figures 5 and 6 ) expand the quantitative picture of Section 5 across multiple entropy estimators and text-diversity metrics. Figure 7 examines whether the filtering advantage is uniform across the four document domains or concentrated in particular content types. Figure 8 provides a mechanistic explanation for the failure of H L H_{L} -based filtering by characterising the generation-0 H L H_{L} distribution.

sections.heading: Three-estimator comparison (Figure 5 ).
sections.text: The main text reports results for H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as the primary collapse metric and briefly notes the H L H_{L} trajectories. Figure 5 places all three estimators – H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , H L Llama H_{L}^{\text{Llama}} , and the independent H L GPT-2 H_{L}^{\text{GPT-2}} scorer – side-by-side across generations, making two patterns visible simultaneously. First, all three estimators agree on direction: the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter condition retains higher entropy than H L H_{L} -filter, which in turn exceeds unfiltered, at generation 6. Second, the H L Llama H_{L}^{\text{Llama}} panel shows the convergence that disables logprob filtering: after generation 0, the three condition means are nearly indistinguishable and their confidence bands overlap almost entirely, so a filter ranking documents by H L H_{L} within a generation operates on noise. The H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} panel exhibits a qualitatively different trajectory, with the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter condition maintaining a visible separation from unfiltered throughout all six generations. Figure 5 : Three entropy metrics across six fine-tuning generations: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} (text-only), H L Llama H_{L}^{\text{Llama}} (Llama-3.1-8B scorer), and H L GPT-2 H_{L}^{\text{GPT-2}} (independent GPT-2 scorer). All three metrics show the same directional ordering at generation 6. The H L Llama H_{L}^{\text{Llama}} panel illustrates why logprob-based filtering fails: after generation 0, the three conditions are nearly indistinguishable, leaving the H L H_{L} -filter little variance to exploit.

sections.heading: Full text-diversity metric suite (Figure 6 ).
sections.text: Table 1 in the main text reports four summary metrics at generation 6. Figure 6 shows trajectories for six metrics across all generations, providing a more complete view of how diversity evolves over the course of the experiment. The within-document metrics (type–token ratio, Distinct-2, Distinct-3, vocabulary size, and Rep-4) all tell a consistent story: the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter condition (green) separates from the other two conditions by generation 1 and maintains a persistent advantage, while the H L H_{L} -filter condition (orange) tracks close to unfiltered on every within-document measure throughout. The Self-BLEU-4 [ Papineni et al., 2002 ] panel (cross-document homogeneity) shows a more complex non-monotonic pattern in early generations, consistent with the discussion in Section 5 : the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter selects a statistically coherent cluster of documents, which briefly increases cross-document similarity. This does not fully resolve by generation 6: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter’s Self-BLEU-4 remains distinctly higher (0.086) than both unfiltered (0.075) and H L H_{L} -filter (0.060, both p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 , Welch’s t t -test) – a small, sustained cross-document homogeneity cost that partly offsets H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering’s much larger within-document diversity gains reported in Table 1 . Figure 6 : Six text-diversity metrics across generations under the three conditions. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering (green) maintains higher diversity on all within-document metrics (TTR, Distinct- n n , vocabulary, Rep-4). Self-BLEU-4 (cross-document homogeneity) shows a non-monotonic pattern in early generations.

sections.heading: Domain-level breakdown (Figure 7 ).
sections.text: A natural concern is that the aggregate filtering advantage reported in Table 1 could be driven by one domain in which H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} happens to be a particularly good signal, while other domains show little or no benefit. Figure 7 plots H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} trajectories separately for each of the four domains – encyclopedic, scientific, conversational, and creative. The H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter advantage is present and directionally consistent across all four, though the magnitude varies: the gap is largest in the conversational domain (where collapse manifests most severely as phrase-level repetition, the exact phenomenon H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} measures) and smallest in the creative domain. No domain shows the H L H_{L} -filter outperforming unfiltered on H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , confirming that the null result for H L H_{L} -filtering is not an artefact of domain averaging. Figure 7 : Domain-level H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} trajectories under the three conditions. The H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter advantage is consistent across all four domains.

sections.heading: Generation-0 H L H_{L} distribution (Figure 8 ).
sections.text: Section 5 argues that H L H_{L} -filtering fails because the within-generation H L H_{L} variance collapses after a single fine-tuning step, removing the ranking signal the filter depends on. Figure 8 documents the starting state that makes this explanation complete. At generation 0 – documents produced by the base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model before any fine-tuning – the H L H_{L} distribution is wide and bimodal (mean = 3.36 =3.36 , SD = 2.17 =2.17 ). The bimodality reflects topic-dependent model familiarity: the base model assigns low entropy to topics well-represented in its pretraining data and high entropy to unfamiliar topics, producing two distinct modes rather than a smooth unimodal spread. After a single generation of fine-tuning on 40 documents, the distribution collapses to a narrow unimodal regime (SD ≈ 0.13 \approx 0.13 , a 17-fold reduction), where all topics are now equally familiar to the fine-tuned model. From generation 1 onward, every document receives a similar H L H_{L} score, so the H L H_{L} -filter’s ranking is determined by noise rather than signal. The wide generation-0 distribution also explains why the H L H_{L} -filter is uncorrelated with H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} at generation 0 ( r = 0.18 r=0.18 , p = 0.11 p=0.11 , Section 3 ): the bimodal H L H_{L} variation captures topic familiarity, not document diversity. Figure 8 : Generation-0 H L H_{L} distribution. The base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model exhibits a wide, bimodal H L H_{L} distribution (mean = 3.36 =3.36 , std = 2.17 =2.17 ), driven by topic-dependent familiarity. After one fine-tuning step the distribution collapses to a narrow regime (std ≈ 0.13 \approx 0.13 ), eliminating the variance the H L H_{L} -filter relies on.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.01493v1 [cs.CL] 01 Oct 2026 No Model Required: Text Entropy Rate Filtering Mitigates Iterative Fine-Tuning Collapse Lewis Mitchell Affiliation: Adelaide Data Science Centre Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences Affiliation: Adelaide University Affiliation: Adelaide SA 5005, Australia Email: lewis.mitchell@adelaide.edu.au Abstract Iterative fine-tuning on synthetic data causes model collapse : output diversity narrows as rare patterns are progressively lost, a signature most visible as phrase-level repetition. Existing mitigations either require model log-probabilities, an external oracle, or continued access to real human data. Here we develop a new approach grounded in mathematical information theory: the non-parametric Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , computed entirely from raw text via match-length statistics, with no model of any kind. We show that this is in fact a superior training-data filter on text-diversity metrics in a fully-synthetic, single-lineage fine-tuning setting. In a six-generation QLoRA collapse experiment on Llama-3.1-8B, logprob-based filtering (the most established model-access-requiring baseline) provides no significant text-diversity benefit on any metric ( p > 0.23 p>0.23 ), whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering yields + 42 % +42\% unique trigrams, + 30 % +30\% vocabulary, and − 19 % -19\% repetition (all p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). We validate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a cross-domain entropy proxy ( β = 0.924 \beta=0.924 , R 2 = 0.746 R^{2}=0.746 ) and collapse detector ( ρ = + 0.454 \rho=+0.454 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ) across 4 domains, 2 temperatures, 2 generator–scorer model pairs, and 1,520 generated documents. Our results demonstrate that information theoretic approaches to collapse mitigation are efficient, and suggest new approaches for maintaining multi-agent diversity. 1 Introduction Large language models trained on their own outputs face a self-reinforcing degradation known as model collapse : when a model’s outputs are used to fine-tune successor models, the entropy of the output distribution declines across generations, diversity narrows, and rare linguistic patterns are progressively lost ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ) . As synthetic content becomes an increasing fraction of web-scraped training corpora, collapse mitigation is shifting from a theoretical concern to an engineering requirement for production training pipelines. Existing mitigations for model collapse fall into one of three categories: (A) model logprob filters such as surplexity filtering ( Gambetta et al., 2026 ) , which scores documents by the model’s own per-token Shannon entropy and retains those the model finds surprising; (B) external oracle or classifier approaches utilising an independent language model; and (C) data accumulation strategies that re-inject real human data at each generation ( Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Bertrand et al., 2024 ) . Among filtering approaches that do not require the injection of real, expensive human data, surplexity filtering is the most established model-access-requiring baseline. Gambetta et al. (2026) demonstrate that it delays collapse as measured by the model’s own entropy and perplexity scores, but its effect on independent text-diversity measures has not been evaluated. Throughout this paper we compare against mean per-token Shannon entropy H L H_{L} specifically, which is closely related to but not necessarily identical to surplexity: both are monotonically increasing functions of the model’s output entropy, but surplexity uses the sample surprise of the generated tokens whereas H L H_{L} averages over the full output distribution, so the two induce highly similar but not necessarily identical document rankings. Moreover, Guo et al. (2024) find that linguistic acceptability filtering can actually worsen collapse, underscoring that the choice of filtering criterion is consequential. Surplexity filtering requires a forward pass through the model being trained, with access to the full next-token distribution at each position. Such access is unavailable for closed-source APIs, computationally expensive at scale, and version-dependent – the same document receives different surplexity scores as the model is updated. Data accumulation avoids model access but presupposes a continuing supply of human-authored text, which is costly and slow to generate, and unavailable in a fully synthetic closed loop. A text-only collapse filter that requires no model of any kind would be strictly preferable, even if it were found to be less effective than surplexity filtering. Motivated by results from mathematical information theory, we propose the Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ( Kontoyiannis et al., 1998 ) as a text-only collapse filter and show that it outperforms logprob-based filtering. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} estimates the entropy rate of a symbolic sequence by measuring match lengths: at each position, it records the length of the longest prefix of the remaining text that has previously appeared in the document. Long matches signal repetition in the text; short matches signal novelty. The Kontoyiannis estimator has previously been used to quantify information flow in social media text ( Bagrow et al., 2019 ; Bagrow and Mitchell, 2018 ; Pond et al., 2020 ) and requires no model, no API, and no GPU. To our knowledge, no prior work has applied H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} or any compression-rate statistic as a collapse filter; it is the only proposed filter of this type requiring no model of any kind – not a forward pass, not an oracle, not a reference classifier. Figure 1 : Filtering on text-only entropy preserves diversity; logprob-based filtering does not. (a) Kontoyiannis entropy rate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} across six fine-tuning generations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under three training-data conditions: unfiltered (rapid collapse), H L H_{L} -filtered (intermediate), and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtered (slowest decline). Shaded bands: ± 1 \pm 1 SEM ( n = 80 n=80 documents per generation). (b) Percentage change relative to the unfiltered baseline at generation 6 for three text-diversity metrics (Distinct-3, Vocabulary size, Rep-4). Error bars: bootstrap 95% CIs. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -based filtering yields highly significant improvements on all three metrics ( ∗ ∗ ∗ p < 0.001 {}^{***}p<0.001 ), whereas H L H_{L} -based filtering is non-significant on all three. Figure 1 previews our central result. In a six-generation QLoRA fine-tuning experiment on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) , each generation’s model is fine-tuned from the previous one – a continuous model lineage reflecting the realistic deployed scenario – and the filter operates in a fully synthetic closed loop with no human data available for re-injection. H L H_{L} -based training-data filtering – the most established model-access-requiring baseline – provides no significant text-diversity benefit on any measured metric ( p > 0.23 p>0.23 ), whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -based filtering yields highly significant improvements ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) on Distinct-3, vocabulary size, and repetition rate – despite H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} requiring no model access at all. The two filters select substantially different training documents (mean within-domain Jaccard similarity ≈ 0.35 \approx 0.35 ), indicating that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is not merely approximating surplexity but operating on a complementary axis: resistance to phrase-level repetition, the primary surface manifestation of fine-tuning collapse. We validate H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} through three experiments: establishing it as a proxy for logprob entropy across domains, temperatures, and model pairs (Section 3 ); characterising when it does and does not track collapse (Section 4 ); and demonstrating that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -based filtering outperforms logprob-based filtering in a controlled iterative fine-tuning experiment (Section 5 ). We release our code and data for reproducibility 1 1 1 https://github.com/lewismath/no-model-required . 2 Background and Related Work Model collapse. Shumailov et al. (2024) demonstrate that iterative training on model-generated data causes progressive loss of distributional tails: output variance shrinks across generations as the model reinforces its existing biases. The phenomenon is formalised by Alemohammad et al. (2024) , who show that without real-data anchoring, iterative self-distillation inevitably converges to low-entropy output. Briesch et al. (2023) provide the first LLM-specific empirical study of self-consuming training loops, finding that diversity declines in proportion to the synthetic data fraction. Measuring collapse in terms of text-level diversity is a more recent development: Guo et al. (2024) conduct iterative fine-tuning on NLG tasks and track lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity across generations, observing that syntactic diversity deteriorates fastest and creative tasks are most vulnerable. Both works characterise collapse through output distribution statistics; we measure it directly via the entropy rate of the generated text. Analogous diversity collapse has been documented in multi-agent LLM systems, where structural coupling during iterative interaction drives premature semantic convergence even without any weight update ( Chen et al., 2026 ) ; the present work identifies a complementary mechanism operating through the fine-tuning data loop. Mitigating model collapse. Existing mitigations fall into three broad categories, each imposing a distinct requirement on the practitioner. (A) Model-logprob methods. Gambetta et al. (2026) propose surplexity – the product of token-level surprise and perplexity – as a data-quality signal for collapse mitigation. In practice, retaining high-surplexity documents is closely related to filtering by the mean Shannon entropy of the generator’s next-token distribution, which we denote H L H_{L} . This is the text-level analogue of perplexity-based data filtering widely used in large-scale pretraining pipelines ( Wenzek et al., 2020 ) . Zhu et al. (2025) resample tokens whose predicted probability exceeds a threshold from a prior language model, requiring token-level logprobs during generation, while Alemohammad et al. (2024) show that biased or top- K K sampling – retaining only the highest-scoring synthetic samples each generation – can slow collapse when a quality score derived from model internals is available. All three methods require access to the generating model’s output distribution. (B) External-oracle methods. Feng et al. (2025) argue that scaling up with synthesised data requires an external verifier – a stronger model or human annotator – to score and filter synthetic samples. Yi et al. (2025) extend this line with convergence guarantees for verifier-based filtering, but identify a critical caveat: long-run convergence is toward the verifier’s biased knowledge centre, not the true data distribution, unless the verifier is perfect. This finding motivates the search for estimators that introduce no external model bias. (C) Real-data accumulation. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) prove that accumulating all prior real and synthetic data yields a finite error bound and validate this empirically. Bertrand et al. (2024) show that retaining a fixed fraction of real data each generation guarantees stability, and Fu et al. (2025) establish that even a constant proportion of real data ensures convergence in transformers. All three approaches require continued access to human-authored data at each training round. Each type of mitigation thus requires either model internals (A), a stronger external model (B), or curated human data (C), imposing an extra burden to mitigate model collapse regardless of the approach taken. In this work we introduce a novel filter in category (D): H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is computed from raw text alone – no model, no API, no GPU, no reference corpus – making it, to our knowledge, the only completely model-free and reference-free model collapse filter proposed to date. Relationship to data deduplication. Min-hash near-deduplication ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Penedo et al., 2024 ) is the standard model-free text-quality filter in large-scale pretraining pipelines, and is the one existing method that, like H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering, requires neither model access nor an external verifier. It removes near-duplicate documents from the training corpus (a between-document operation), whereas H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering selects documents by within-document phrase variety (a within-document operation). The two approaches are complementary: deduplication prevents the corpus from containing many copies of the same text, while H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering ensures each document has not collapsed into internally repetitive structure. A combined pipeline (deduplicate first, then H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter) would address both failure modes. The Kontoyiannis estimator. Kontoyiannis et al. (1998) prove that the estimator H ^ K = n ​ log 2 ​ n ∑ i = 1 n Λ i \hat{H}_{K}=\frac{n\log_{2}n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Lambda_{i}} (1) converges almost surely to the entropy rate H H of any stationary ergodic process – no parametric assumptions on the token distribution are required – where Λ i \Lambda_{i} is the length of the shortest prefix of x i , … , x n x_{i},\ldots,x_{n} that does not appear as a contiguous substring in x 1 , … , x i − 1 x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1} ; near the end of a document, where no such non-appearing prefix may exist, Λ i \Lambda_{i} is bounded by the remaining sequence length n − i n-i , so the sum in Equation ( 1 ) remains well-defined without special-casing. Reported H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} values use the ProcessEntropy package’s tokenizer 2 2 2 https://github.com/tobinsouth/ProcessEntropy : an NLTK TweetTokenizer pass, lower-cased, with non-alphanumeric characters stripped from within each token ( South et al., 2022 ) . Real-time filtering decisions during fine-tuning (Section 5 ) instead use a faster whitespace tokenization (lower-case; non-alphanumeric characters replaced with whitespace) for computational efficiency; the two agree closely in practice (Spearman ρ = 0.997 \rho=0.997 on a held-out sample), so the choice does not affect which documents are selected. The estimator’s consistency is grounded in the Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem ( Cover and Thomas, 2006 ) : for a stationary ergodic source, − 1 n ​ log 2 ⁡ P ⁡ ( X 1 , … , X n ) → H -\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}P(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\to H almost surely, and Λ i \Lambda_{i} serves as a nonparametric proxy for local self-information at position i i – long matches signal low surprise; short matches signal high surprise. The match lengths also connect H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} to Lempel–Ziv (LZ) data compression ( Ziv and Lempel, 1977 ; Ziv and Lempel, 1978 ) : each Λ i \Lambda_{i} identifies the shortest phrase at position i i not resolvable from prior context – the elementary step of LZ parsing – so H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is interpretable as a normalised LZ compression rate. While compression-based statistics have been used for general data quality assessment, to our knowledge no prior work has applied H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} or any LZ-derived metric as a model collapse mitigation filter. At finite n n , H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is upward-biased: early positions have little past context, so Λ i \Lambda_{i} is artificially small and the denominator is deflated. We control for this by computing H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} on the first 1,500 word tokens of each document and discarding shorter texts (see Section 3 ); the residual finite-sample bias is reported as a limitation in Section 6 . The Kontoyiannis estimator provides a model-free measure of sequential complexity that depends only on the text itself ( Bagrow et al., 2019 ; Smart et al., 2024 ) . Fine-tuning. We use QLoRA ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) – 4-bit NF4 quantisation with low-rank adaptation ( Hu et al., 2022 ) – for all fine-tuning experiments. QLoRA makes multi-generation fine-tuning tractable on a single A100 GPU, enabling the iterative collapse and filtering experiments described in Sections 4 and 5 . 3 H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a Proxy for Logprob Entropy We first ask whether H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is a suitable proxy for H L H_{L} , by comparing the two metrics on a set of synthetic documents. 3.1 Cross-domain and cross-temperature validation We generated 200 documents using GPT-4o across 4 domains (encyclopedic, creative, scientific, conversational), 2 temperatures ( T ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 } T\in\{0.5,1.0\} ; higher temperatures were excluded in preliminary testing because too large a fraction of sampled tokens fell outside the top-20 returned logprobs), and 25 topics per domain; 197 documents passed a reliability filter requiring that fewer than 5% of a document’s tokens have unrecoverable (invalid) logprob coverage. For each document we computed H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} via Equation ( 1 ) applied to the first 1,500 word tokens, and H L H_{L} , the mean per-token Shannon entropy of the generator’s next-token distribution, renormalised over the top-20 returned logprobs. An OLS regression of H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} on H L H_{L} with domain fixed effects yields β = 0.924 \beta=0.924 ( R 2 = 0.746 R^{2}=0.746 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ; Figure 2 a shows the T = 1.0 T=1.0 subset). A likelihood-ratio test for domain-specific slopes fails to reject equality ( p = 0.41 p=0.41 ), confirming a domain-invariant slope : the relationship between H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} is consistent across domains up to a domain-level intercept offset. Domains differ in baseline entropy – creative and conversational text is more varied; scientific text more constrained – but H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} scales with H L H_{L} at the same rate in each. The domain-invariant slope has a practical consequence for data filtering. Because filtering requires only the rank order of documents by entropy (selecting the top- k k ), not absolute calibration, a single H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} computation suffices for within-domain ranking. In a mixed-domain corpus, domain stratification remains necessary to prevent over-selection from naturally higher-entropy domains. 3.2 Cross-model validation The cross-domain experiments above use the same model (GPT-4o) for both generation and H L H_{L} scoring. Here we test whether the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} / H L H_{L} relationship holds when H L H_{L} is computed by a different model family altogether. We generated additional corpora using Gemini 1.5 Pro ( Gemini Team, Google, 2024 ) and scored all documents – both GPT-4o-generated and Gemini-generated – using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) as an independent scorer. Both the GPT-4o/Qwen and Gemini/Qwen pairings reproduce the positive H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} / H L H_{L} relationship (Figure 2 b), confirming that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} measures a property of the text itself, not of any particular model’s distribution over that text. 3.3 Scope: proxy validity on collapse-experiment data The validations above use text generated under controlled conditions (varied temperature, well-distributed topics). To assess whether the relationship extends to the data used in the collapse experiment itself, we compute H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} on the 80 generation-0 documents produced by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (the base model, before any fine-tuning). The correlation is near zero and non-significant ( r = 0.18 r=0.18 , p = 0.11 p=0.11 , n = 80 n=80 ). This is not a failure of the estimator but a known property of the base model’s output distribution: as documented in Figure 8 , the base Llama model produces a wide bimodal H L H_{L} distribution (SD = 2.17) driven by topic-dependent familiarity rather than document-level diversity. Within each topic, H L H_{L} is nearly constant; between topics it varies by up to 7 bits. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , which measures within-document phrase variety, is orthogonal to this between-topic variation. The proxy relationship holds when H L H_{L} reflects genuine document-level entropy variation, but not when it is dominated by topic-familiarity confounds – and this is the root cause of H L H_{L} -filtering’s failure in Section 5 . (a) Cross-domain validation: GPT-4o corpus ( T = 1.0 T=1.0 , n = 97 n=97 ). (b) Cross-model validation: GPT-4o and Gemini corpora, both scored by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Figure 2 : H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} versus H L H_{L} across domains and model pairs. Points are coloured by domain. The slope is domain-invariant in both panels: H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} scales with H L H_{L} at a consistent rate regardless of domain, generating model, or scoring model. 4 Detecting Model Collapse Without Logprobs Having established H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a cross-sectional proxy for H L H_{L} , we next ask whether it tracks collapse over generations . Under iterative rephrasing, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} co-decline at indistinguishable rates ( δ = − 0.004 \delta=-0.004 , p = 0.59 p=0.59 ), but within-generation rank concordance is near zero (Spearman ρ ≈ 0 \rho\approx 0 ), as rephrasing homogenises surface statistics across documents and eliminates the variance needed to discriminate between estimators. The fine-tuning regime is more informative, as we explore below. 4.1 Iterative fine-tuning collapse Fine-tuning collapse operates through a different mechanism than rephrasing. Rather than paraphrasing existing content, the model’s generative style drifts: text exhibits increased phrase repetition, reduced vocabulary diversity, and narrower syntactic range (see examples in Appendix A ). We conducted a 6-generation QLoRA fine-tuning experiment (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, unfiltered training data) and computed within-topic H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} / H L H_{L} concordance across generations for each of 39 topics (one topic was excluded due to insufficient within-generation variance for reliable rank correlation). Under fine-tuning collapse, within-topic Spearman concordance is ρ = + 0.454 \rho=+0.454 ( p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ), with 30 of 39 topics showing positive concordance (Figure 3 b). This contrasts sharply with the rephrasing scenario ( ρ = − 0.175 \rho=-0.175 , non-significant). The explanation is that fine-tuning collapse changes the surface statistics of generated text in ways H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} directly measures – repetitive phrase structure, reduced n n -gram diversity – whereas rephrasing preserves the within-generation homogeneity that masks both estimators. This result establishes H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a valid detector of fine-tuning collapse specifically, and motivates its use as a filter in that regime. (a) Iterative rephrasing collapse: mean ± \pm SEM of H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} across rephrasing generations. Both estimators decline together ( δ = − 0.004 \delta=-0.004 , p = 0.59 p=0.59 ). Shaded region: gen-0 reference (length-mismatched). (b) Iterative fine-tuning collapse: within-topic Spearman ρ \rho under fine-tuning collapse. Each point is one topic; diamonds show domain means. Figure 3 : H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a collapse detector under two regimes. Under rephrasing (a), H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} co-decline but within-generation concordance is ≈ 0 \approx 0 . Under fine-tuning (b), within-topic concordance is strongly positive ( ρ = + 0.454 \rho=+0.454 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ), driven by phrase-level repetition that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} directly measures. 5 H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} as a Training Data Filter Having established that H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} is a good collapse detector, we now consider our central question: can H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} be used to filter training data and mitigate collapse; and, if so, does it outperform H L H_{L} , the most established model-access-requiring baseline? 5.1 Experimental design We run three parallel 6-generation QLoRA fine-tuning chains on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. At each generation, 80 documents are generated across 4 domains (10 topics × \times 2 documents per topic per domain); 40 are selected for training according to the condition: Unfiltered : random selection (seed fixed per generation); H L H_{L} -filter : top 40 by mean per-token Shannon entropy (logprob-based surplexity; see Section 1 for the distinction between H L H_{L} and surplexity proper); and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filter : top 40 by Kontoyiannis entropy rate (text-only). Selection is domain-stratified (10 documents per domain), so both filters operate within domain. Generation-0 documents are drawn from the base model and are shared across conditions. Training uses 4-bit NF4 QLoRA (rank 16, α = 16 \alpha=16 , learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , cosine schedule, 3 epochs per generation, effective batch size 8). Documents selected for training are truncated at the onset of 4-gram repetition; this preprocessing does not apply to generated outputs, which are evaluated as-is (see Appendix A ). The experiment produces 1,520 documents in total: 80 shared generation-0 documents plus 3 conditions × \times 6 further generations × \times 80 documents. Reproducibility.
