The Kontoyiannis estimator directly penalises repeated phrase structure: a document with many recurring n n -grams exhibits long match lengths and hence a low H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} . Fine-tuning collapse manifests primarily as increased phrase repetition, so H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering targets collapse’s dominant surface signature directly. H L H_{L} , by contrast, measures token-level uncertainty in the scorer model – a signal that is destroyed after a single fine-tuning step, as shown in Section 5 . At generation-0, H L H_{L} primarily reflects topic familiarity – the wide bimodal distribution documented in Figure 8 – rather than document diversity, so a criterion uncorrelated with document quality at generation-0 cannot select high-quality training data regardless of downstream variance. The result suggests that collapse is fundamentally a phrase-repetition phenomenon, and that phrase-level statistics are better positioned to detect it than token-level uncertainty. A literal reimplementation of surplexity confirms this mechanistic prediction directly: its median absolute deviation across the shared generation-0 pool is 4.40 4.40 , falling to 0.40 0.40 – 0.49 0.49 (all three conditions) after one fine-tuning step – a 9 9 – 11 11 -fold narrowing, comparable to H L H_{L} ’s own collapse. (Generation-0 surplexity is heavy-tailed – a handful of unfamiliar-topic documents receive extreme values once surprise is exponentiated into perplexity – so median and MAD, not mean and SD, are the meaningful summary here.) Filter design determines direction of effect. Not all filters slow collapse: Guo et al. (2024) find that linguistic acceptability filtering (a RoBERTa classifier trained on CoLA) accelerates diversity decline, since such filters retain conventional, high-frequency text and discard the inventive samples most worth keeping. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering operates on the opposite principle, selecting for the phrase-level novelty that collapse erodes. The Jaccard gap and Simpson’s paradox. The reason why the two filters select such different documents (Jaccard ≈ 0.35 \approx 0.35 ) when H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} and H L H_{L} are well-correlated at the corpus level ( R 2 = 0.746 R^{2}=0.746 ) is a form of Simpson’s paradox. The between -domain correlation is strong: creative and conversational text have both high H L H_{L} and high H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ; scientific text has both low. But within a domain and generation – which is where filtering operates, due to domain stratification – the residual correlation is near zero. The estimators measure genuinely different properties of intra-domain text variation; H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s phrase-level novelty proves more informative for collapse resistance. Practical implications. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} filtering requires no model access, no API calls, and no GPU: scoring a 1,500-word document takes under 10 ms, and a pipeline producing 10 5 10^{5} candidate documents per round incurs negligible, trivially parallelisable overhead. This makes collapse-resistant data curation practical where logprob access is unavailable: closed-source API distillation, cross-organisation data sharing, and federated training. Limitations. Most importantly, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering preserves text diversity but does not protect general reasoning ability: HellaSwag accuracy degrades equally across all three filtering conditions (Figure 4 b), and MMLU and GSM8K show the same pattern, so our claim is scoped to distributional fidelity of generated text, not downstream task performance. The filtering advantage is also specific to fine-tuning collapse: under iterative rephrasing, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} tracks the aggregate trajectory but cannot distinguish among documents within a generation, and is therefore unsuitable as a within-generation filter in that setting. The diversity gains measured here are lexical: MAUVE scores ( Pillutla et al., 2021 ) (GPT-2-Large features, first 512 tokens) are near-ceiling and uniform across conditions at generation 6 ( 0.987 0.987 – 0.993 0.993 ), indicating embedding-space similarity is preserved and H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} ’s advantage is specific to within-document match-length structure. A separate concern is quality: selecting for match-length novelty could favour incoherent or off-topic text over genuinely diverse text. We address this directly with an LLM-judge pass (GPT-4o-mini, blind to condition) scoring all 240 generation-6 documents (80 per condition) on two 1–5 scales, coherence and instruction-following, reading the full document so that late-document degeneration is not missed. H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering scores highest of the three conditions on both: coherence 2.35 2.35 versus 2.20 2.20 for unfiltered ( p = 0.058 p=0.058 ) and 2.29 2.29 for H L H_{L} -filtering; instruction-following 3.23 3.23 versus 3.00 3.00 for unfiltered ( p = 0.020 p=0.020 ) and 3.15 3.15 for H L H_{L} -filtering. If anything, then, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering’s diversity advantage comes with a small quality benefit rather than a coherence cost. Finally, our collapse experiment uses a single model family (Llama-3.1, 8B); replicating with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (same corpus and protocol), H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering again retains more diversity at generation 6 ( 2.91 2.91 bits/word versus 2.12 2.12 unfiltered, p < 0.001 p<0.001 , and 2.41 2.41 for H L H_{L} -filtering, p = 0.004 p=0.004 ; H L H_{L} -filtering again non-significant on all text-diversity metrics), with the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -vs- H L H_{L} comparison itself reaching significance on the H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} metric ( p = 0.004 p=0.004 vs p = 0.088 p=0.088 at 8B), providing stronger evidence the two filters are genuinely different. Beyond replication, the Kontoyiannis cross-entropy rate h ^ × ​ ( T ∣ S ) \hat{h}_{\times}(T\mid S) is a natural complement to H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} , selecting for documents that have diverged from prior-generation content; the same signal could operationalise – as an automatic, text-only proxy – the blind-writing independence phase Chen et al. (2026) identify as the most effective structural intervention against diversity collapse. Broader impacts. The primary benefit is making collapse-resistant data curation accessible without model access, reducing a practical barrier for organisations running iterative fine-tuning under closed-source or resource-constrained conditions, and counteracting homogenisation of AI-generated web content. The main negative consequence is indirect: making fully-synthetic training pipelines more viable may reduce the incentive to collect or compensate human-authored training data; practitioners deploying such pipelines at scale should weigh this trade-off. 7 Conclusion We have shown that the Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} – a model-free, match-length measure of sequential complexity – is an effective training-data filter against fine-tuning-driven model collapse: at generation 6 it produces 42 % 42\% more unique trigrams, 30 % 30\% larger vocabulary, and 19 % 19\% less intra-document repetition than unfiltered training, while logprob-based filtering shows no significant diversity benefit. For iterative pipelines where model internals are inaccessible, H ^ K \hat{H}_{K} -filtering offers a strong, zero-cost baseline.
